articles.title: Prediction, Prescription, and Proactive Medication Management in the Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: This narrative review examines the evolving role of prediction analytics in comprehensive medication management for critically ill patients. Intensive care unit pharmacotherapy is challenged by medication complexity, physiologic instability, heterogeneous treatment response, and continuous data streams. Predictive systems may support proactive medication management by identifying medication-related harm, therapeutic failure, optimization opportunities, and pharmacist workload earlier in the patient trajectory. The review discusses medication-informed prediction models, prescriptive analytics, workload-aware critical care pharmacist allocation, and potential future applications. Implementation requires actionable predictions, workflow integration, clinician oversight, and attention to equity, safety, and model credibility.
articles.authors: Murray Brian

articles.title: Intensive Monitoring, Big Data, and Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care.
articles.abstract: Intensive care is defined by providing a higher level of patient monitoring, but only a fraction of the data created through continuous hemodynamic monitoring are captured in the electronic health record. The monitoring data that is captured misses clinically important deterioration events and is not adequate to represent critical illness physiology for care at the bedside or for research. This article describes the current state of patient monitoring in intensive care, advanced monitors in development, metadata and its role in creating rich intensive care data sources, and machine learning and its current and future applications in intensive care medicine.
articles.authors: Rzewnicki Daniel I, Bhavani Sivasubramanium V

articles.title: Redesigning Intensive Care Unit Workflows: A Learning Health System Approach to Improving Care Delivery.
articles.abstract: Critical care leaders are increasingly asked to improve outcomes, reduce burden, and implement evidence-based care in complex, highly interdependent clinical environments. Meeting this challenge requires redesigning the workflows through which care is delivered, not simply measuring outcomes or adding new tools. This article presents a learning health system model that integrates sociotechnical systems thinking, quality improvement, health services research, and informatics to support workflow redesign. Multidimensional workflow signals inform the Diagnose, Redesign, Implement, Verify, Evolve (DRIVE) cycle to make care delivery more reliable, less burdensome, and better aligned with outcomes that matter to patients.
articles.authors: Murphy David J

articles.title: Optimizing Team Integration of Critical Care Pharmacists: Where We Go Next.
articles.abstract: Critical care pharmacists (CCPs) are essential members of the intensive care unit team who provide comprehensive medication management to improve patient outcomes, safety, and cost efficiency. This article highlights barriers to optimal integration of CCPs within multidisciplinary teams as well as opportunities to address them. Persistent barriers include financial, workforce, data, interprofessional, and regulatory. Strategies to address these gaps may involve standardized metrics, innovative staffing models, and research to strengthen evidence-based implementation. Metrics should include all members of the Stakeholder Triad and should include a mix of workload metrics, safety and efficacy metrics, and work-design metrics.
articles.authors: Smith Susan E, Henry Kelli, Papadopoulos John, et al.

articles.title: Optimizing Team Integration of Critical Care Pharmacists: A History of Critical Care Pharmacy Practice and Evolving Definition of "Optimal Practice".
articles.abstract: Critical Care Pharmacists (CCPs) are essential members of the intensive care unit (ICU) team who provide comprehensive medication management to improve patient outcomes, safety, and cost efficiency. This article highlights best practices for optimal CCP integration, including optimal patient-to-pharmacist ratios, participation in interprofessional rounds, team-based practice models, and expanded coverage across all shifts. The Triple Domain framework is useful to evaluate CCP value across patients, health care teams, and institutions. Best practices include an ICU patient-to-CCP ratio of less than or equal to 15:1 and inclusion of CCPs on daily interprofessional rounds.
articles.authors: Smith Susan E, Bektas Aeryana N, Henry Kelli, et al.

articles.title: The COVID-19 Pandemic as a Stress Test of the Intensive Care Unit Workforce.
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic monumentally strained the intensive care unit (ICU) workforce and revealed both the strengths and vulnerabilities in contemporary critical care delivery. In this review, we briefly describe the composition of the US ICU workforce and the organizational features most relevant to staffing. Next, we examine how the pandemic disrupted critical care delivery, specifically health care workers. Finally, we discuss the lasting psychological toll and workforce attrition; highlight adaptations that emerged, such as tele-ICU expansion, virtual family engagement, tiered staffing models, rapid-onboarding curricula, and peer support programs; and outline priorities for policy, practice, and research to strengthen workforce resilience.
articles.authors: Connell Kathryn A, Vranas Kelly C, Yu Hyunmin, et al.

articles.title: The Intensive Care Unit Team: Roles, Scope, and Interprofessional Interdependence in the Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: A hallmark feature of an intensive care unit (ICU) is the presence of a structured team-based interprofessional model. Although composition of the ICU team varies by organization and patient population, it typically includes critical care nurses, intensivists, respiratory therapists, and clinical pharmacists. Interprofessional teams in ICUs are associated with increased collaboration and improved patient outcomes. However, the ICU team faces challenges in workforce shortages, staffing gaps, and ineffective information sharing, which can inhibit effective team function. Proven strategies to support collaboration among the ICU team include structured interprofessional rounds, strong leadership of the team, care protocols, and quality bundles.
articles.authors: Manzo Laura L, Christoph Ella N I, Kessinger Stephanie K, et al.

articles.title: Streamlining the Evidence-to-Practice Pathway With Computerised Decision Support in Anaesthesiology and Critical Care: A Qualitative Study of Clinician and System-Level Interest Holder Perspectives Across Five Scandinavian Countries.
articles.abstract: Implementing evidence-based recommendations in anaesthesiology and critical care remains challenging due to guideline, workflow and contextual barriers. Guideline-based computerised clinical decision support systems (CDSS), embedded in structured pathways linking international guidelines to Scandinavian-endorsed recommendations and delivered via electronic health records, may help strengthen the evidence-to-practice pathway. This study aimed to explore perceived barriers and facilitators to their use. This qualitative study interviewed 10 clinicians (anaesthesiologists and intensivists; specialists and non-specialists; < 40 and ≥ 40 years; male and female) and nine system-level stakeholders (hospital and health authority representatives) from Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. We integrated endorsed international guidelines into a CDSS providing patient-specific reminders linked to recommendations, as well as shared decision-making tools and decision-analytic components. articles.title: A Survey of Clinician-Reported Management of Hypernatremia in the ICU.
articles.abstract: Hypernatremia is frequent in the intensive care unit (ICU) and is associated with adverse outcomes. Despite its prevalence, robust evidence to guide treatment is lacking, and global practice patterns are largely unknown. We investigated global treatment preferences and clinicians' willingness to enroll patients in a randomized trial to inform its feasibility. This international cross-sectional online survey comprised 20 primarily closed-ended questions, using five-point Likert-scale responses, across four themes: treatment method, threshold, correction rate, and opinion on a proposed trial. Respondents considered a clinical vignette of hypernatremia developing before or during ICU admission, excluding dehydration and chronic causes. It was distributed to ICU physicians worldwide. The survey was sent to 3053 ICU physicians in 17 countries, with 1051 respondents, yielding a response rate of 34%. Of respondents, 74% were consultants, and 26% were residents. articles.title: Serious Adverse Events in Adult ICU Patients: A Substudy of the PATIENCE Cohort.
articles.abstract: Prokinetic agents are used to enhance upper gastrointestinal motility, but adverse events related to these agents are poorly described. We aimed to provide detailed epidemiological data on predefined serious adverse events (SAEs) in a cohort of adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients with and without prokinetic treatment. We hypothesised that all predefined SAEs would occur in both patients treated and those not treated with prokinetic agents, and that a higher number of SAEs would occur among patients treated with prokinetic agents for more than three consecutive days. This substudy of the inception cohort study "Prokinetic agents in adult intensive care unit patients" included acutely admitted adult ICU patients. The prokinetic agents assessed (exposures) were erythromycin, metoclopramide, domperidone, and prucalopride. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients experiencing at least one episode of five pre-specified SAEs during ICU stay (cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, vomiting with aspiration, diarrhoea, extrapyramidal symptoms). articles.title: Discussing Future Treatment and Care in the ICU: Perspectives From Patients.
articles.abstract: Treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) is usually predicated on curative treatment, but continuing all available treatment options may not always be beneficial for the patient or in line with their wishes. However, patients admitted to the ICU are often assessed as incapable of making decisions regarding their care; hence conversations about wishes for treatment are postponed. This study aimed to investigate the experiences of patients who participated in a conversation concerning treatment and care following ICU discharge based on the Danish version of the Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment (ReSPECT) form. Semi-structured telephone interviews were conducted with patients who had a conversation about future treatment and care with an intensivist using the ReSPECT form during an ICU admission between November 2024 and July 2025. articles.title: Swedish Consensus Recommendation for Follow-Up After ICU Stay.
articles.abstract: A substantial proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) survivors experience long-term physical, psychological and cognitive impairments after critical illness. However, methods for identifying patients in need of post-ICU support vary widely. As a result, many patients are left without access to established rehabilitation pathways. This consensus recommendation provides a framework for the organisation and content of follow-up for adult ICU survivors in Sweden, informed by available evidence, stakeholder perspectives and expert consensus. The National System for Knowledge-Driven Healthcare Management (NPO) in Sweden commissioned the development of a practice recommendation for the follow-up of critically ill adults. Multidisciplinary experts in ICU survivorship formed a task force group. A systematic literature search in four databases was conducted in 2024 to identify pre-existing systematic reviews on the topic. The literature was reviewed, assessed for quality and recommendations were developed based on the literature evidence. articles.title: How are researchers using MIMIC? A sampling-based methods review.
articles.abstract: The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) database is a widely used open data resource in critical care research. Its accessibility has led to large numbers of research studies being published; however, design and analysis decisions made by individual studies may vary, affecting comparability and reproducibility. We conducted a sampling-based methods review of research that analysed the MIMIC database. Studies published between 2015 and 2025 were eligible for inclusion in the sampling frame. A random sample of 100 eligible studies was identified through the OpenAlex bibliographic database; data were collected using a structured extraction framework. Information was extracted on study aims, cohort definitions, exclusion criteria, outcome specification, handling of missing data, and analytical methods. The review focused on how key design and analytical decisions were reported and justified in the random sample. Studies reported findings from general ICU and specific clinical populations; the study population could not be determined for 32 of the 100 studies. articles.title: Analysis of work system components in interprofessional communication to determine shock etiology.
articles.abstract: In critical care settings, lack of agreement among clinicians on shock etiology is associated with higher mortality. Effective interprofessional communication may facilitate agreement on etiology and reduce mortality. This study sought to understand the interaction of work system components (people, environments, tools, tasks) in interprofessional communication to determine shock etiology. We interviewed 28 physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses, and pharmacists at three United States hospitals using a Critical Incident Technique. Analysis was guided by the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety model. The principal finding was that clinicians worked across fragmented physical, socio-organizational, and digital environments to balance the urgency to treat shock with intermediate steps to reduce diagnostic uncertainty. The results suggest that future research should acknowledge the benefits of productive disagreement among clinicians and develop supports that promote synchronous communication by bridging physical and socio-organizational fragmentation, compiling and systematizing relevant clinical information, and generating shared awareness among clinicians.

articles.title: Training of trainers on medical education reforms: a prospective multicenter French survey among intensivists.
articles.abstract: The recent reform of the second cycle of medical education in France introduced competency-based medical education (CBME) with the incorporation of several pedagogical modalities into undergraduate training and assessment, including objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs), simulation-based teaching (SBT), and clinical reasoning (CR) instruction throughout the academic year. While these tools are central to preparing competent practitioners, their effective implementation depends on adequately trained educators. We hypothesized that training would be insufficient, notably in the recently introduced pedagogical modalities. We conducted a national, cross-sectional survey (June-September 2023) to assess the level and adequacy of training of board-certified physicians practicing in critical care and involved in undergraduate teaching. An anonymous online questionnaire collected demographic data, teaching frequency, training characteristics, perceived adequacy and usefulness of training, preparedness, and barriers. articles.title: Beyond the ICU: family resilience and emotional turmoil after intensive care - a qualitative study.
articles.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, visitation restrictions in ICUs intensified psychological distress among family members, yet the long-term impact of psychosocial support on family resilience remains poorly understood. To evaluate the experiences of family members during the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on interactions with healthcare professionals and well-being 18th months after hospitalisation. A qualitative descriptive study using semi-structured interviews with 14 families of patients admitted to the ICU in spring 2020.Data were analysed using inductive content analysis. Experiences were shaped by caring interactions with healthcare professionals, emotional disruption, and reliance on family support. Clear information and psychosocial support fostered trust but were also associated with stress and feelings of isolation. articles.title: Intensive Care Unit Management of the Hemodynamically Significant Pulmonary Embolism.
articles.abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, with prognosis determined by right ventricular (RV) adaptation to the abrupt rise in pulmonary vascular resistance. Although most cases can be managed outside the intensive care unit, patients with RV failure, hemodynamic instability, or cardiac arrest require advanced monitoring and intervention. Management in this setting emphasizes rapid diagnosis and risk stratification, timely initiation of reperfusion therapies, and carefully tailored hemodynamic and respiratory support. Optimal outcomes rely on multidisciplinary collaboration, early escalation of care, and individualized, evidence-based decision-making.
articles.authors: Ehret Jane, Langston Matthew D, Friedman Oren

articles.title: Higher Daily Hospitalization Costs and Intensive Care Utilization Among Decedents With Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Bioethical Analysis of End-of-Life Care.
articles.abstract: End-of-life care creates financial burdens. This study examines medical procedures/interventions and costs for inpatients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), comparing those who died during hospitalization to those who survived, analyzing the findings through a bioethical perspective. This observational 1:1 case-control study was conducted at a tertiary care center. Patients with SLE and RA (ICD-10-CM diagnostic codes) who were hospitalized for at least 24 h during two distinct periods-January-June 2019 and January-June 2023-were included. Patients were designated as cases if they died during hospitalization and as controls if they were discharged alive. Data were abstracted from electronic medical records using standardized formats. Microcosting data for each hospitalization were obtained from the accounting department. We identified 29 matched pairs of cases and controls, primarily comprising middle-aged females, with SLE. articles.title: Artificial intelligence and continuous renal replacement therapy.
articles.abstract: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is an important intervention in the treatment of acute kidney injury (AKI) in intensive care, and its application scope continues to expand alongside technological advancements and an increasing patient population. However, in current clinical practice, several factors, including individual patient differences, dynamic treatment needs, and the rational allocation of medical resources, pose challenges to CRRT implementation. The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) offers new approaches to address some of these challenges, and its applications in developing decision-support models, refining workflows, and supporting patient communication and education may contribute to more precise and efficient CRRT management. In this article, we discuss the current evidence and potential applications of AI in CRRT, as well as the challenges and strategies for clinical implementation, aiming to provide a reference for future research and clinical translation of AI-assisted CRRT. articles.title: Irritant Contact Dermatitis Related to Fecal and Urinary Incontinence in the Critical Care Population.
articles.abstract: Irritant contact dermatitis due to fecal, urinary, or dual incontinence is a common but often under recognized complication in critically ill patients that contributes to pain, skin breakdown, infection, and pressure injury risk. Despite advances in understanding its prevention and management, practice remains variable. This article contrasts traditional and evidence-based approaches, reviewing terminology, risk factors, pathophysiology, diagnosis, and interventions. A practical critical care application of the Manage→Clean→Protect→Restore care bundle, adapted from the 2026 Wounds International Best Practice Update, is presented to support standardized, proactive incontinence skin care, and improve patient outcomes.
articles.source: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
articles.authors: Hutton Jennifer L

articles.title: Temperature Measurement in the Acute Care Setting.
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients often suffer from alterations in body temperature either from disease, injury, exposure, or therapeutic interventions. Therefore, nurses must use evidence to guide decisions in choosing the most appropriate thermometer, route, and technique that accurately and consistently reflects core body temperature. This article will review the evidence for measuring body temperature for critically ill patients. Practical recommendations for measuring body temperature will follow.
articles.source: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
articles.authors: Timmerman Rosemary

articles.title: Revisiting Rest: Evidence-Based Shifts in Adult Intensive Care Unit Early Mobility.
articles.abstract: Improvements in intensive care unit (ICU) survival have highlighted the long-term burdens faced by survivors, including physical, cognitive, and psychological impairments. Immobility is a key contributor to these outcomes. Over the past 2 decades, ICU practices have shifted from deep sedation and bedrest toward early mobility and patient engagement. ICU early mobility (EM) is an evidence-based intervention that is safe and feasible. However, implementation remains inconsistent. This article explores the historical context of ICU bedrest, reviews current evidence supporting ICU EM, and offers strategies for its adoption.
articles.source: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
articles.authors: Dunn Heather, Lavrenz Danielle, Yousef Shaimaa, et al.

articles.title: Intensive Care Unit Liberation: Transforming Critical Care Through the ABCDEF Bundle.
articles.abstract: This article highlights the shift from traditional intensive care unit practices, including deep sedation, immobility, and restricted visitation, to evidence-based, patient-centered care. These outdated methods, once considered protective, are now known to increase delirium, muscle weakness, cognitive decline, and health care costs. Implementing the ABCDEF bundle (eg, pain management, awakening and breathing trials, sedation choice, delirium management, early mobility, and family engagement) is a proven evidence-based framework that improves patient outcomes. Critical care nurses play a central role in driving bundle adherence. Successful implementation requires interdisciplinary teamwork, leadership support, education, and integration into practice standards.
articles.source: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
articles.authors: Gregory Stephanie, Ratliff Erika

articles.title: Aligning Peripheral Intravenous Catheter Practices with the Vessel Health and Preservation Framework.
articles.abstract: The Vessel Health and Preservation framework was established with the aim of increasing the implementation of evidence-based vascular access practices and ultimately improving patient outcomes. This model was designed to place attention on reducing infection risks and drive more effective assessments of site selections, appropriate device selection, and increased application of strategies that reduce vascular harm, complications, and patient discomfort. Many conventional nonevidence informed practices with peripheral intravenous catheters continue to persist in critical care. Understanding best evidence to guide vascular access will positively impact patient safety and outcomes.
articles.source: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
articles.authors: Wenger Barbara, Seyller Nicole, Varty Maureen

articles.title: Deimplementation of Tradition-Based Enteral Feeding Practices to Improve Clinical Outcomes.
articles.abstract: Enteral feeding is common in acute and critical care but there are many elements to this practice that are steeped in confusion and lack evidence. This article will focus on verification of feeding tube (FT) placement methods and timing, medication administration by FTs, unnecessary holding or stopping of enteral formula, gastric residual volumes, and volume-based feeding. Supporting evidence for these practices will be reviewed and recommendations made for evidence-based alternatives and possible deimplementation.
articles.source: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
articles.authors: Bourgault Annette M, Powers Jan

articles.title: Culture and the Intensive Care Unit Team: Factors Driving Teamwork, Safety, Quality, and Well-Being.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) culture and teamwork strongly influence health care quality, patient safety, clinical outcomes, and clinician well-being. Culture shapes how multidisciplinary clinicians communicate, coordinate care, and adopt new practices. Persistent variability in ICU practices, including end-of-life care, sedation management, and mobility, often reflect differences in local culture and team dynamics. Emerging perspectives from complexity science, network science, and behavioral economics conceptualize the ICU as a complex adaptive human network in which collective behavior patterns emerge through repeated clinician interactions. Understanding ICUs through this lens may provide tools, processes, and strategies to improve health care delivery.
articles.authors: Fuchita Mikita, McPeake Joanne, Mikkelsen Mark E

articles.title: Administrative Harm and Workforce Strain Indicators.
articles.abstract: The way work is structured within health care, from work environments to workloads, shapes both the workforce experience as well as job performance. Administrative harm describes the downstream effects of upstream decisions on the design of work itself, impacting workforce well-being and performance, patient care and outcomes, and organizational outcomes. The article reviews current and emerging opportunities to harness digital signals readily available within the electronic health record (EHR), including EHR use metadata and related data sources, to measure, monitor, and predict how work design (job demands and resources) affects workforce, patient, and organizational outcomes.
articles.authors: Leventhal Kara-Grace, Caudill Darren, Moss Marc, et al.

articles.title: Intensive Care Unit Staffing Ratios: Evidence, Experience, Economics, and Execution.
articles.abstract: The clinician-to-patient ratio is a simple construct which can be useful in strategizing for intensive care unit (ICU) staffing. Evidence is limited and inconsistent, but overall suggests such ratios may impact patient outcomes, clinician experiences, and health system economics. Importantly, however, ICU clinicians function as part of an interprofessional team, and no single staffing metric can be considered in isolation. As such, no one-size-fits-all approach to clinician-to-patient ratios exists. Yet, typical ranges are now known and decisions to operate outside of these ranges should be done with care, at least until new evidence can better guide practice.
articles.authors: Gershengorn Hayley B, Buckley Mitchell S, Costa Deena K, et al.

articles.title: Moral Distress, Burnout, and the Intensive Care Unit Environment.
articles.abstract: This article examines the relationship between moral distress and burnout among intensive care unit (ICU) clinicians and argues that moral distress acts as a precursor to burnout. Moral distress arises when clinicians cannot act according to ethical obligations due to systemic constraints, leading to cumulative moral residue. In high-intensity ICU environments, this distress is driven by nonbeneficial treatment, poor communication, and resource limitations. Over time, unresolved moral distress contributes to chronic workplace stress and burnout. The authors emphasize that system-level interventions, particularly ethics consultation and organizational change, are essential to address root causes and improve clinician well-being and patient care.
articles.authors: Epstein Elizabeth G, Bourne Dawn, Taylor Julia F

articles.title: Valvular Shock in the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit: Perioperative Care for Transcatheter Valve Interventions.
articles.abstract: Valvular heart disease is an uncommon but high-risk cause of cardiogenic shock requiring rapid, multidisciplinary management aimed at bridging patients to definitive surgical or transcatheter valve intervention. Early comprehensive Doppler echocardiography is essential, as clinical signs may be subtle. Distinguishing decompensated chronic valvular disease from acute unstable lesions guides urgency and treatment strategy. Medical stabilization and mechanical circulatory support vary markedly between stenotic and regurgitant lesions, and standard shock therapies may be harmful in specific contexts. Transcatheter approaches are preferred when feasible, though their expanding use introduces added complexity in cardiac intensive care.
articles.authors: Prosperi-Porta Graeme, Dahiya Garima, Hibbert Benjamin, et al.

articles.title: Integrating Tummy Time Into Routine NICU Care: Healthcare Workers' Perspectives on Long-Term Implementation in India.
articles.abstract: Prone positioning for play ('Tummy Time') is an evidence-based recommendation that supports early sensory-motor development during infancy. Infants who require neonatal intensive care face a heightened risk of motor developmental delays, underscoring the importance of early developmental care practices. Routine implementation of tummy time remains limited in many settings in India and is not included in national guidelines. Socio-cultural factors further influence the adaptation of such a cost-effective intervention in India. In response, a structured tummy time practice was introduced at discharge from the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) of a tertiary-care hospital in India in 2016. This study explored multidisciplinary NICU healthcare workers' perspectives on implementing tummy time, including its perceived feasibility, acceptability and long-term integration into routine practice. articles.title: Therapeutic drug monitoring of meropenem in human serum using a sensitive four-electrode electrochemical biosensor for critically ill patients in intensive care wards.
articles.abstract: Therapeutic drug monitoring of antibiotics in critically ill patients with sepsis remains challenging due to highly variable pharmacokinetics, increasing the risk of under- or overdosing. This paper presents a novel single-use tetrapolar electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) biosensor for the rapid detection of meropenem in human serum. The sensor is based on a gold microband electrode functionalised with a self-assembled monolayer, protein G and anti-meropenem antibodies to enable selective antigen capture and impedance-based quantification. The biosensor demonstrated sensitive detection of meropenem over a range of 1-100 μg/mL in phosphate-buffered saline and within clinically relevant concentrations (8-16 μg/mL) in spiked human serum, with the lowest measured concentration of 1 μg/mL. Binding specificity was validated using tandem mass spectrometry and immunocapture liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. The total assay time was under 15 min. This platform represents a promising approach for rapid, bedside-compatible monitoring of meropenem. articles.title: Presepsin outperforms conventional biomarkers for Sepsis diagnosis and 30-day mortality prediction: A multicenter prospective study in a north African ICU cohort.
articles.abstract: Sepsis remains a leading cause of intensive care unit (ICU) mortality, necessitating the identification of accurate biomarkers for diagnosis and prognosis. Presepsin (sCD14-ST), generated through monocyte/macrophage phagocytosis of bacterial components, offers infection-specific signals. This study compared the diagnostic and prognostic performance of with of procalcitonin (PCT), C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and interleukin-8 (IL-8) within the same patient cohort. This prospective multicenter cohort study enrolled 184 participants across two Algerian tertiary ICUs: 60 healthy controls, 30 patients with pulmonary infection, 46 with sepsis, and 48 with septic shock (Sepsis-3 criteria). All biomarkers were measured using a single blood sample collected within six hours of admission. Diagnostic accuracy was assessed using ROC curve analysis and DeLong's test, and independent predictors of 30-day mortality were identified using binary logistic regression. articles.title: Voices from the neonatal unit: Mothers' and healthcare workers' perspectives on respectful and collaborative care for small and sick newborns in rural districts in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa.
articles.abstract: Neonatal care increasingly emphasizes improving the experience of care by engaging mothers as active partners alongside health workers providing clinical care for newborns. Guided by the World Health Organization's Standards for improving the quality of care for small and sick newborns, this study focuses on Standard 4, which promotes care that is respectful, responsive, and supportive of families' needs and preferences. We conducted a concurrent triangulation mixed-methods study among health workers and mothers of small and sick newborns admitted to neonatal units in two rural districts of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Effective communication emerged as a foundational factor shaping mothers' experiences of care. Many mothers reported frustration due to inadequate, unfriendly communication and exclusion from clinical decision-making, resulting in limited collaboration and lack of informed consent. A secondary exploratory objective was to assess the discriminative performance of a multivariable logistic regression model incorporating these four variables. This retrospective cohort study included 345 singleton pregnancies complicated by PPROM and managed at a tertiary care centre between January 2020 and December 2025. The four prespecified variables were entered simultaneously into a multivariable logistic regression model to evaluate their independent associations with NICU admission. articles.abstract: Neonatal palliative care is an essential component of care for the most vulnerable infants and their families, yet its provision in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) remains inconsistent, in part due to gaps in nurse education and training. This project evaluated the effect of a brief, introductory palliative care education program on NICU nurses' knowledge and communication self-efficacy. A one-group pretest-posttest design was used at a private hospital NICU in northern California, where 25 NICU nurses completed a 20-minute self-study video and a small-group role-play session covering the SPIKES and NURSE communication tools. A 10-item investigator-developed survey measured knowledge and self-efficacy at baseline, immediately after training, and 4 weeks later. Mean self-efficacy scores rose from 16.7 at baseline to 19.2 immediately after training and 20.1 at 4-week follow-up, with statistically significant immediate and lasting gains in self-efficacy and overall scores (P < .001), although knowledge gains did not reach statistical significance. articles.title: Short-chain fatty acid metabolism in acute lung injury and intervention strategies from traditional Chinese medicine.
articles.abstract: Acute lung injury (ALI) and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) are severe conditions associated with high mortality rates and limited treatment options. Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) serve as central immunomodulatory metabolites mediate the crosstalk between the gut and lung. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), with its holistic approach, shows promise in restoring gut-lung balance and alleviating respiratory inflammation by modulating gut microbiota and SCFA metabolism. To elucidate the protective role and mechanism of SCFAs in ALI and ARDS via the gut-lung axis. Meanwhile, to evaluate the therapeutic potential of TCM in treating ALI by modulating the gut microbiota and enhancing SCFA production. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, Ovid-Embase, Web of Science, and CNKI databases (2010-2025). Keywords included "short-chain fatty acid", "gut microbes", "acute lung injury", "traditional Chinese medicine", and related terms. articles.title: Herpesvirus reactivation in critical illness: Pathogenesis, clinical consequences, and diagnostic challenges.
articles.abstract: Human herpesviruses (HHV) remain latent after primary infection and may reactivate during critical illness. HHV reactivation has been associated with adverse clinical outcomes, yet its pathogenic significance and optimal management remain unclear. This review summarizes the dysregulated immune mechanisms and risk factors for HHV reactivation in critical illness, treatment options, outcomes, current diagnostic challenges, and emerging precision medicine approaches. Critical illness induces profound immune dysregulation characterized by an initial hyperinflammatory response followed by immunosuppression, T-cell exhaustion, impaired natural killer cell function, and disrupted antiviral surveillance. These changes facilitate reactivation of latent HHV, including herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6). articles.title: Cross-kingdom microbiome interactions along the gut-lung axis: immune-microecological coordination, shared mechanisms, and disease-context dependence in respiratory disorders.
articles.abstract: Cross-kingdom dysbiosis of the gut microbiome along the gut-lung axis has emerged as a key driver of chronic and acute respiratory diseases. Beyond bacteria, the intestinal mycobiome and virome, including bacteriophages, shape mucosal immunity and metabolism through partially overlapping but non-redundant pathways. In this Review, we synthesize rapidly expanding evidence that fungi, bacteria, and phages in the gut form an integrated network that may influence susceptibility, inflammatory tone, and therapeutic responsiveness across asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and lung cancer via the gut-lung axis. We first summarize how cross-kingdom communities in the intestine are organized and interact, highlighting a tripartite framework centered on pathogen-associated molecular pattern-pattern recognition receptor (PAMP-PRR) circuits, the short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-regulatory T-cell axis, and tryptophan-indole-aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) signaling. articles.title: The Pharmacologic Management of Cardiac Arrest.
articles.abstract: The effectiveness of pharmacologic management of cardiac arrest patients is widely debated; however, several studies published in the past 5 years have begun to clarify some of these issues. This article covers the current state of evidence for the effectiveness of the vasopressor epinephrine and the combination of vasopressin-steroids-epinephrine and antiarrhythmic medications amiodarone and lidocaine and reviews the role of other medications such as calcium, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium, and atropine in cardiac arrest care. We additionally review the role of β-blockers for refractory pulseless ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation and thrombolytics in undifferentiated cardiac arrest and suspected fatal pulmonary embolism.

articles.title: Endpoint-specific mortality associated with malignancy among adults with sepsis or septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a major global health challenge and increasingly affects patients with complex conditions such as malignancy. Prior studies suggest higher mortality in this population, but interpretation is limited by aggregation of heterogeneous endpoints. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to clarify endpoint-specific prognostic associations between malignancy and mortality in adults with sepsis or septic shock. This study was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251141216). PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and Epistemonikos were searched through 16 September 2025, for studies comparing all-cause mortality between sepsis patients with and without malignancy. Mortality endpoints were grouped as ICU, in-hospital, early, intermediate and extended follow-up mortality. Crude odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup, meta-regression and sensitivity analyses were performed to explore heterogeneity and assess consistency. articles.title: Peripheral Vasopressor Administration: An Evidence-Based Risk-Benefit Analysis.
articles.abstract: Peripheral vasopressor administration has been heavily researched over the past decade as a way to quickly treat hemodynamically unstable patients. However, current evidence is diverse and limited by quality concerns, including a reliance on retrospective studies, inconsistent criteria, and bias risk. While central venous access devices (CVADs) remain the preferred route for vasopressor administration, use of the peripheral route is necessary when a CVAD is not yet present or contraindicated. Vascular access selection should be tailored to individual patient's needs. Current evidence indicates that using a protocolized approach for peripheral vasopressors appears safe and effective for low-acuity patients requiring short-term therapy (eg, less than 24 hours).

articles.abstract: Ventilation is provided to most patients during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). International guidelines emphasize the need for effective intra-arrest ventilation while acknowledging uncertainty regarding the optimal ventilation parameters. This review will discuss how new studies challenge prior beliefs on key ventilation parameters, will highlight challenges and potential solutions for high-quality ventilation and will suggest a translational research approach to advance intra-arrest ventilation. A recent observational study reported that higher ventilation rates during in-hospital cardiac arrest may be positively associated with return of spontaneous circulation, challenging common beliefs. Additionally, a pivotal observational study on bag-valve-mask ventilation during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest found that ventilation was frequently ineffective and if so, associated with reduced survival and neurological function. articles.title: Prone positioning in acute respiratory distress syndrome: A critical review of clinical evidence and practical challenges.
articles.abstract: Early randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of prone positioning (PP) in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) failed to demonstrate a survival benefit despite consistent improvements in oxygenation. Subsequent meta-analyses suggested a survival advantage in patients with severe hypoxaemia, culminating in the landmark Proning Severe ARDS Patients (PROSEVA) trial, which reported a 28-day mortality rate of 16.0% in patients with a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio <150 mmHg. However, the optimal criteria for repeating and discontinuing PP sessions remain uncertain. A structured search of PubMed, Embase.com, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) was conducted to identify RCTs evaluating PP in adults with ARDS with mortality as a prespecified principal outcome. Relevant clinical studies, meta-analyses, and review articles were also evaluated to provide context for the narrative review. Six RCTs were included in the main comparative analysis. articles.abstract: Acute lung injury (ALI) and its severe form acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) are critical conditions with few effective therapies. Triptolide (TPL), a bioactive compound from Tripterygium wilfordii, exhibits potent anti-inflammatory effects but its clinical use is restricted by poor solubility, rapid clearance, and hepatotoxicity. Using network pharmacology and molecular docking as hypothesis-generating approaches, we prioritized NLRP3 inflammasome activation as a key candidate pathway mediating the therapeutic effects of TPL against ALI. articles.title: Management of shock phenotypes after cardiac arrest: beyond cardiogenic shock.
articles.abstract: Postcardiac-arrest circulatory failure is commonly labeled cardiogenic shock, although its physiology is heterogeneous, dynamic, and frequently mixed. This review examines recent evidence and proposes a treatment-oriented framework. Hypotension, hyperlactatemia, vasopressor dependence, and myocardial dysfunction do not establish ongoing shock after cardiac arrest or identify its mechanism. Recent studies demonstrate clinically important discordance between arterial pressure, cardiac output, filling pressures, oxygen transport, metabolic recovery, and prognosis. Four primary hemodynamic phenotypes are proposed: vasoplegic-inflammatory shock; myocardial dysfunction and low-flow shock; hypovolemia; and right ventricular and pulmonary vascular dysfunction. Mixed shock is an overlap group, whereas reversible metabolic pseudoshock describes arrest-related hyperlactatemia that resolves without persistent hemodynamic compromise. articles.abstract: Sepsis remains a major global health challenge. A multinational modified Delphi study was conducted with 164 experts from 22 countries, 12 specialties, and 105 scientific societies. articles.abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) has a high mortality rate. European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) and American Thoracic Society (ATS) Guidelines are the worldwide reference for clinicians in management of ARDS. articles.abstract: Myocardial injury in severe community-acquired pneumonia (SCAP) is often under-recognized, and interpretation of high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) may be complicated by renal dysfunction and critical illness. We evaluated whether admission interleukin-8 (IL-8) and soluble suppression of tumorigenicity 2 (sST2) could support early risk stratification of guideline-consistent myocardial injury in patients with SCAP. In this prospective cohort of 146 patients with SCAP, guideline-consistent myocardial injury was defined as hs-cTnI elevation above the assay-specific 99th percentile upper reference limit. Admission IL-8, sST2, and their combination were assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis and 10-fold cross-validation. Fixed and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)-stratified hs-cTnI thresholds were compared in an exploratory analysis. An exploratory subgroup analysis was performed among patients with CURB-65 ≤ 1. The median age was 71 years; 91 patients (62.3%) were male and 55 (37.7%) were female. articles.title: [Emergency medicine requirements for the resuscitation room and the resuscitation room team].
articles.abstract: The resuscitation room is the central interface between prehospital emergency medical services (EMS) and in-hospital emergency care for critically ill and severely injured patients. From an EMS perspective, requirements are defined for activation, prenotification, team structure, handover, overload management and feedback. Written activation and allocation criteria are required that are applicable in the prehospital setting and agreed upon by hospitals, emergency dispatch centres and EMS providers. Prenotification must take place through a continuously available, reliable communication channel, be actively acknowledged and enable transparent feedback on capacity. Paramedics must be authorised to activate the resuscitation room independently of the presence of an emergency physician. On arrival, a qualified and operational team with clearly identifiable roles should be available. Handover should be structured and as interruption-free as possible. The exploratory online survey showed that trauma resuscitation care is predominantly guideline-based and more often includes a written minimum staffing requirement. articles.title: The efficacy and safety of micronutrient complementation in adults during the acute phase of critical illness: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients often experience metabolic imbalances and potentially low micronutrient blood levels that worsen oxidative stress and impair immune function. Despite guideline recommendations, micronutrient complementation is inconsistently applied due to accessibility issues and the lack of validated assessment tools during acute critical illness. This retrospective cohort study evaluated the impact of early intravenous micronutrient complementation on clinical outcomes in ICU patients using real-world electronic medical record data. Adult ICU patients at National Taiwan University Hsinchu Branch from July 2024 to November 2025 who received parenteral nutrition (PN) for at least 24 hours were included. Patients were divided into a treatment group receiving micronutrients within 72 hours of ICU admission and a control group without complementation. Primary outcomes included in-hospital mortality and infectious complications after day 6 of PN; secondary outcomes included ICU/hospital length of stay, inflammatory and metabolic biomarkers, organ support needs, and refeeding syndrome incidence. articles.abstract: Next of kin of critically ill patients frequently experience distress. Although family needs have been associated with psychological outcomes, their potential role as a pathway linking clinical and relational factors to emotional distress remains poorly understood. To examine whether family needs mediate the relationships between ventilatory support, relationship to the patient and emotional distress among the next of kin of critically ill patients. A cross-sectional study was conducted in an adult Intensive Care Unit in Portugal between September 2024 and February 2025. Emotional distress was assessed using the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scales-21 and family needs using the Family Needs Inventory in the Intensive Care Unit. Mediation analysis was performed using maximum likelihood estimation with bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals (5000 resamples). articles.title: Clinical nutrition for critically ill patients: A practical appraisal of guideline gaps and perspectives for future research.
articles.abstract: Malnutrition and accelerated muscle wasting are frequent during critical illness and make nutritional support a central component of ICU care. Nutritional support is therefore central to ICU care, but its optimal timing, route, dose, and composition remain debated. Recent randomized trials have challenged the traditional objective of early full feeding and shifted practice toward progressive, phase-adapted, and tolerance-based nutrition. This narrative review compares current international guidelines for nutritional support in critically ill adults. Guidelines broadly agree that nutrition should be initiated early after clinical stabilization, acute-phase overfeeding should be avoided, energy and protein delivery should be increased progressively, and refeeding syndrome should be anticipated. However, important differences remain regarding acute-phase energy targets, protein dosing, enteral versus parenteral nutrition, supplemental parenteral nutrition, indirect calorimetry, and enriched enteral formulas. articles.abstract: Persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome (PICS) is a phenotype of chronic critical illness characterized by unresolved inflammation, impaired immune competence, sustained catabolism, skeletal muscle loss, recurrent infections, and poor functional recovery. Although guideline-based nutritional support remains fundamental, persistent immunometabolic abnormalities may limit responsiveness to nutrient delivery and contribute to anabolic resistance, impaired substrate utilization, and defective tissue repair. This mini-review examines biological mechanisms limiting nutritional responsiveness in PICS and evaluates evidence for pathophysiology-guided nutritional strategies. articles.abstract: Constipation is a common complication in critically ill patients and has been associated with adverse clinical outcomes. However, the role of enteral nutrition composition, particularly fiber and fluid administration, remains unclear. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between dietary fiber and fluid administration and constipation in invasive mechanical ventilated critically ill adults. We conducted a prospective cohort study including 74 critically ill adults requiring invasive mechanical ventilation and enteral nutrition. Patients were followed for up to 144 h from initiation of mechanical ventilation. Fiber and total fluid administration were evaluated as time-varying exposures. articles.title: Nutrition management in critically ill surgical patients: a clinical practice guideline appraisal and synthesis.
articles.abstract: Critically ill surgical patients are particularly vulnerable to inadequate nutritional intake due to surgery, trauma, treatment-related interruptions, and hypermetabolic stress. Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) are important for guiding nutritional management in this population, but specific recommendations remain limited. Therefore, this systematic review aimed to evaluate the methodological quality of CPGs related to nutritional management in critically ill surgical patients and to synthesize their recommendations. Comprehensive bibliographic searches were conducted across six literature databases and ten guideline repositories to identify CPGs published between January 2005 and November 2025. Professional society websites and relevant grey literature sources were also searched. Data on guideline characteristics and development methodology were extracted. articles.title: Individualizing post-ICU nutrition: from guideline intent to bedside practice.
articles.abstract: Survivorship of critical illness has increased, shifting attention toward recovery and long-term outcomes. Post-ICU nutrition is emerging as a clinically relevant, yet underperforming contributor to functional recovery and quality of life. Persistent nutritional inadequacy reflects insufficiently defined physiological requirements and limited implementable evidence-based guidance during ICU recovery. Energy and protein delivery sharply decline after ICU discharge, despite persistent metabolic demands. Underfeeding can result from the absence of recovery-specific targets, patient-level barriers (e.g. appetite loss, dysphagia, fatigue), and fragmented care transitions, including premature feeding-tube removal and suboptimal monitoring of oral intake. Structured patient and family engagement can help operationalize individualized nutritional strategies and improve feasibility without substantial resource burden, acting as continuity agents. articles.abstract: Exposure keratopathy is an ocular surface injury caused by prolonged corneal exposure, most often from incomplete eyelid closure. Critical illness can intensify exposure through reduced blinking, chemosis, impaired corneal reflexes, sedation, mechanical ventilation, and tear film instability. This narrative clinical review synthesizes contemporary evidence on epidemiology, mechanisms, risk factors, bedside assessment, prevention, protocol implementation, and care in resource-constrained intensive care units (ICUs). PubMed/MEDLINE was searched for English language literature from January 2000 through 15 September 2026, supplemented by reference list and guideline searches. Systematic reviews, randomized trials, cohort studies, quality improvement reports, and relevant guidance were prioritized. articles.abstract: Recognizing its clinical utility, the 2024 Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guideline recommends using equations that integrate serum creatinine and cystatin C for CKD diagnosis and staging. Cystatin C-inclusive equations generally outperform creatinine-based equations in bias and accuracy across diverse populations, including children and patients with comorbidities. Moreover, cystatin C-inclusive equations consistently demonstrate greater prognostic value than creatinine-only equations for clinical outcomes such as kidney failure with replacement therapy, cardiovascular disease, and mortality, particularly in individuals with large differences between creatinine-based and cystatin C-based eGFR. Among hospitalized patients and those undergoing significant changes in muscle mass, such as during weight loss or critical illness, cystatin C may improve GFR estimation and facilitate earlier detection of AKI. In clinical practice, cystatin C informs CKD staging, risk stratification, and medication dosing, particularly in scenarios where creatinine-based equations are less reliable. articles.abstract: Acute hypoxemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure are among the most common reasons for ICU admission and need for invasive mechanical ventilation. Noninvasive respiratory support (NIRS) strategies-including high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC), noninvasive ventilation (NIV), and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)-may prevent intubation, improve outcomes, and reduce ICU utilization. However, there is uncertainty regarding optimal patient and modality selection, resulting in variable implementation. There are no clinical practice guidelines comprehensively addressing the use of the different NIRS strategies across the spectrum of acute respiratory failure. articles.title: Intravenous Vitamin C and Mortality and Organ Dysfunction in Severe Burn Injury
articles.abstract: To the Editor We read with interest the article from the recent VICTORY trial that reported increased mortality in patients with severe burns who were randomized to 4-day administration of vitamin C vs placebo. The rationale for vitamin C administration was the massive release of oxygen free radicals following severe burns. However, the median time to discharge alive from the intensive care unit was 42.5 days in the placebo group, suggesting that a 4-day course of vitamin C may have been too short to affect outcomes. Notably, 2 previous randomized clinical trials in critically ill patients reported that abrupt discontinuation of a 4-day course of vitamin C was associated with increased mortality.
